title: HarnessTax: Does Your Claude Need Claude Code?
html:
HarnessTax: Does Your Claude Need Claude Code?

Melissa Z. Pan1, Shuo Yang1, Negar Arabzadeh1, Wei-Lin Chiang2, Ion Stoica1, Matei Zaharia1

1 UC Berkeley · 2 Arena Intelligence Inc.

Language models are changing how we build software and solve computational problems1,2. Coding agents put these capabilities to work through harness, a software system that manages a model’s tools, context, and task execution3. While models provide the core intelligence behind coding agents, harnesses are increasingly seen as central to how effectively that intelligence is used and extracted3,4. Choosing a coding agent therefore means choosing both a model and a harness, even when the explicit focus is only on the model.

Millions of people already use coding agents. OpenAI reported more than 5 million weekly active Codex users in June 2026, and Anthropic reported that Claude Code’s weekly active users doubled in the first six weeks of 2026.5,6 Programming also accounted for more than half of OpenRouter’s token volume by late 2025.7 But the impact of harness choice remains unclear. What does the harness actually add, and at what cost?

One missing piece is understanding of how the model and harness work together. Performance reports for Anthropic models in Claude Code or GPT models in Codex tell us how each pair performs. Could the same model solve more tasks, or achieve the same success at lower cost, in another harness?

We evaluate 21 model–harness pairs spanning seven models and three harnesses—Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Pi—on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0.8,9 Our study reveals three key findings:

  1. Harness choice affects cost more than task success on the benchmarks we test. The same model can achieve similar success rates at substantially different costs.
  2. A minimal harness can be competitive. Pi shows that a simpler, open-source harness can be competitive on both cost and task success.
  3. Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness. A model’s provider does not necessarily offer its most effective pairing. So it turns out that your Claude models may not need Claude Code…

We examine each finding below and will publicly release our profiling traces.

Experiment Setup

We compare 21 model–harness pairs on the same 30 randomly sampled tasks from each benchmark: SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. We run each pair three times per task to capture variation between attempts. We start with each harness’s native configuration, cap each attempt at 100 turns, and select its corresponding high effort setting. Turn counts and effort settings follow each harness’s own definitions. We measure task success using each benchmark’s official evaluator.

Measurement details. We first average cost and success over each task’s three attempts, then average across the 30 tasks. We estimate 95% confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Each resample draws 30 task averages with replacement and recomputes the overall mean. We compute token cost using a fixed direct-API price list dated September 1, 2026, applying the same prices to each model across harnesses.

We explicitly disable two web search related default tools in Claude Code (WebFetch and WebSearch) and use an empty, strict MCP configuration. In Codex, we disable web search with web_search="disabled". Pi has no default web tool to disable. We also configure the API gateway to reject hosted tool declarations (web_search, web_fetch, mcp, computer, and image generation) in every request. Each task container is created with --network=none and joins a relay namespace that also has no external network access. This blocks external network access through shell commands such as curl, pip download, and git fetch for every model.

For Pi, we install two additional packages to configure subscription keys and control agent turns.

We access Kimi K3 via Fireworks AI. Kimi K3 has a single native thinking mode on our gateway, so the effort field does not change its thinking mode. All three harnesses therefore use the same mode for Kimi K3.

(1/3) Harness affects cost more than correctness.

The same model often achieves a similar success rate at substantially different costs. GPT-5.6 Luna offers the lowest cost on both benchmarks, while Claude Fable 5 reaches the highest success rate on SWE-bench Lite. Kimi K3 as an open-weight model sits on Pareto frontier of SWE-Bench Lite, and just sits right below Pareto frontier on Terminal-Bench 2.0 . However, these models do not have substantial performance differences when changing across harnesses. Claude Fable 5 solves 94.3% of attempts in Claude Code, 93.1% in Codex and 93.1% in Pi, yet Claude Code costs about twice as much per attempt as Pi ($1.29 vs $0.64).

Figure 1. Token cost and success rate for 13 model–harness pairs on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. Each marker averages 90 attempts: three attempts on each of 30 randomly sampled tasks. Colors identify models; marker shapes identify harnesses. The stepped line marks the observed Pareto frontier: no evaluated alternative improves cost or success without worsening the other. Use the model buttons to highlight a model’s results across harnesses and the harness buttons to show each harness’s Pareto frontier.

Fable 5 with Claude Code achieves the highest accuracy on Pareto than with Pi by 1.1% but at 1x more cost on SWE-Bench Lite. The cost gap extends beyond Fable 5. Across shared models, Claude Code costs about 2.1× as much as Pi and 1.8× as much as Codex on SWE-bench Lite, and 1.5× as much as Pi on Terminal-Bench 2.0, using geometric means of cost ratios. Meanwhile, the average harness effect on success rate stays within ±2% on SWE-bench Lite and within ±5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

You may be paying a hidden “harness tax” when you accept a coding agent’s default harness without comparing alternatives. Model evaluations should therefore compare the same model’s cost and task success across commonly used harnesses. Results from one harness cannot show whether another could achieve a similar success rate for less.

(2/3) A minimal harness can be competitive.

The natural question, then, is why some harnesses are more efficient than others. We examine cumulative cost–success curves and recorded agent turn counts to investigate these differences.

Figure 2. Cumulative cost–success curves. For each model–harness pair, we sort all 90 completed rollouts by their final cost, grouping equal costs. Each point shows cumulative cost on the x-axis and cumulative successful rollouts on the y-axis, both divided by 90. Failed rollouts add cost without adding success. Curves closer to the upper-left show more cumulative success at lower cost. A nine-point moving average smooths the curves; the unsmoothed endpoint matches the pair’s mean cost and success rate in Figure 1.

Similar agent turns can lead to substantial different costs. For Fable 5 on SWE-bench Lite, Codex and Claude Code have nearly identical agent turns per attempt (15.0 and 15.1), but Claude Code costs 1x more per attempt, with a 1.1% improvement in success rate. Such a cost gap suggests higher average spend per agent turn in Claude Code than Codex.

Pi and Codex show that open-source harnesses can be competitive on the benchmarks we test. Pi reaches the Pareto frontier on both benchmarks with just four default tools: read, write, edit, and bash.10 Codex CLI includes more built-in features, including planning, prompt caching, and automatic context compaction, while remaining cost-efficient.11

![][image3]

Figure 3. Context in the first main model call on SWE-bench Lite. Values are means ± standard deviations across 609 attempts per harness: seven models × \tbd{30} tasks × 3 attempts. We measure instruction and tool-schema lengths in characters and count the tool definitions exposed to the model. Provider-reported input tokens include the task prompt (roughly 0.5k tokens), so they measure total initial context. Codex exposes nine tools for Claude and Kimi models and three to four for GPT models.

A harness tax can begin with the first main model call. Across all seven models, Claude Code’s mean initial context is over 10× Pi’s, with longer instructions and larger tool schemas. Its tool set includes subagent delegation and other orchestration features described in its public documentation.12 This additional context can increase cost, though total spending also depends on caching, generated tokens, and subsequent calls. Higher spending can still accompany higher success: for GPT-5.6 Sol on SWE-bench Lite, Claude Code reaches a higher final success rate than Pi at greater cost.

The effectiveness of Pi and Codex demonstrates opportunities for open harness research with existing models. Researchers can work with SOTA coding harnesses without access to proprietary harnesses or co-training with the model. Richer harness features may still benefit other models, workloads, or interaction settings. Harness complexity should therefore be treated as an empirical trade-off, not an assumed advantage.

(3/3) Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness.

Yes… you’re reading the plot correctly: Opus achieves a higher measured success rate in Codex than in Claude Code, at less than half the cost. On our SWE-bench Lite sample, Opus 4.8 success rates 86.2% of attempts in Codex versus 85.1% in Claude Code, at 28% less price per attempt.

Figure 4. Mean token cost per attempt and success rate for each model across Pi, Codex CLI, and Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. Whiskers show 95% confidence intervals. Green outlines identify each model’s lowest cost and highest success rate separately. The broken cost bar extends beyond the displayed axis.

The result extends beyond Opus and beyond Claude Code. Sonnet 4.6 solves 67.8% of attempts in Codex versus 66.7% in Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite at a similar cost. GPT-5.6 Sol also performs competitively outside its provider's harness: on Terminal-Bench 2.0, it achieves an 83.3% success rate in Pi versus 78.9% in Codex, at half the cost ($0.42 versus $0.84). Across the six Anthropic and OpenAI models and both benchmarks, an alternative harness achieves the highest observed success rate in nine of twelve comparisons.

These results show that a model’s capabilities are compatible, generalizable and can carry over to other harnesses. Providers do report to optimize some models for their own coding environments: OpenAI, for example, describes GPT-5-Codex as optimized for agentic software engineering in Codex.13 Yet we observe that a shared provider does not guarantee the best pairing. The practical question remains which harness delivers the best balance of cost and task success for a given model and workload. And thus evaluation is required for cross harnesses and models.

Your Claude may not need Claude Code after all… 🤔

Ending Notes

HarnessTax shows that the same model can achieve similar success rates at substantially different costs. On the benchmarks we test, minimal open-source harnesses can be competitive, and models can perform well outside their provider’s harness. Choosing a coding agent therefore also means choosing how much we pay to use a model’s capabilities. A harness tax can go unnoticed when we focus only on task success.

More broadly, the need for different harnesses depends on what is the role of coding agents. For day to day coding tasks, the role of harness serves as an efficient interface to tools, context, and execution. Additional guardrails, and features may not be necessary for many tasks. While, harder problems that are at the boundary of pushing model capability may still benefit from more structured support for exploring ideas, evaluating candidates, and learning from feedback.

HarnessTax is a step toward understanding models and harnesses jointly. The next step is to examine whether these patterns hold in real development workflows, where requirements evolve, developers provide feedback, and tasks extend across sessions. Measuring cost and task success alongside developer effort would help establish which harness features earn their cost in practice.
